#1338. The deep Earth origin of the Great Unconformity

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature volume 659, pages 106–112 (2026) Cite this article

The Great Unconformity marks a globally extensive erosive surface linked to climatic shifts1 and environmental transitions2 that preceded the Cambrian explosion of life. The processes proposed to explain the formation of the Great Unconformity include glacial erosion during the Snowball Earth1,3,4, rifting and plume activity5,6,7, sea-level fall8 and mantle-driven dynamic topography6,9,10,11. However, the dynamics of these processes have not been tested. Here we show that continental-scale uplift and subsidence associated with long-wavelength dynamic topography12 due to mantle convection drove the formation and preservation of the Great Unconformity. Our models predict prolonged continental-scale Neoproterozoic uplift and long-term Phanerozoic subsidence for Laurentia, Baltica and North China. This vertical motion scenario is ideal for the formation and preservation of the Great Unconformity, which is a first-order surface expression of deep Earth processes. The predicted prolonged continental uplift throughout Cryogenian times would have resulted in marked erosion due to the action of glaciers13. The large area of Laurentia and limited deformation at its margins explain why the Great Unconformity is best preserved and documented there. Our models predict cycles of dynamic topography that are broadly reflected in preserved sediment volume across continents1,14, and open new avenues for understanding the environments of Cambrian animal diversification.

An unconformity is a surface that represents a temporal gap (hiatus) in the geologic record in which younger sediments are deposited over older rocks, after a period of erosion or non-deposition15. Although unconformities are common in the rock record, they markedly vary in spatial extent and hiatus duration. The largest known unconformity is called the Great Unconformity16. It represents an erosional or non-depositional hiatus lasting about 200 million years (Myr) or longer, and marks the onset of sedimentation at the start of Phanerozoic time and of the Cambrian explosion of life2. The Great Unconformity was first described in the Grand Canyon17, and has been established across North America from a digital database of sedimentary deposits1,2,9 and thermochronological data3,4,6,7,10,18. The oldest sediments at the base of the Great Unconformity in North America are between 635 Myr old and 482 Myr old (Ediacaran to Early Ordovician times; Fig. 1). Spatially extensive unconformities of a similar age have been documented in Baltica19,20,21,22,23,24 and in North China8,25,26,27,28. The global sedimentary volume estimated from geologic maps and borehole data more than doubled across the Precambrian–Phanerozoic boundary1,14.

a,b, The Great Unconformity was formed by continental-scale erosion of Precambrian crystalline basement (a) followed by Cambrian sedimentation (b). In b, the sedimentary strata are coloured by age and the white line represents the Great Unconformity surface. The schematics in a and b are not to scale. c, Spatial distribution of the oldest sedimentary strata deposited between Late Ediacaran and Early Ordovician (Ordo) times in the database Macrostrat55, coloured by age. Lambert azimuthal equal-area projection at the surface of Earth.

The cause or causes of the Great Unconformity are unknown. The proposed mechanisms include extensive glacial erosion during Snowball Earth (about 720–635 Myr ago or Ma)1,3,4, rifting and plume activity5,6,7, sea-level fall8 and mantle-driven dynamic topography6,9,10,11. These processes have not been dynamically tested, with limited comparison between global models and global datasets to explain the spatial distribution of the Great Unconformity. Here, we propose that continental-scale dynamic topography6,9,10,11,12,29,30, which is transient over thousands of kilometres and tens of millions of years12, provided the driving force for surface processes to generate the continental-scale denudation and sedimentation consistent with the geologic record of the Great Unconformity6,9,10,11. Dynamic uplift followed by dynamic subsidence can produce large-scale erosional surfaces and unconformities11,12,31. We test this hypothesis by analysing the evolution of continental dynamic topography predicted by a series of mantle convection models, and comparing it with the volume of sediment preserved on continents over time1,14.

To investigate the deep Earth origin of the Great Unconformity, we considered palaeogeographically constrained mantle convection models from 1 billion years ago (Gyr ago or Ga). Input parameters were varied across a series of six models M1–M6 (Extended Data Table 1). These models were driven by tectonic reconstructions in the no-net-rotation (NNR) frame of reference, except for M3, which was based on a palaeomagnetic (PMAG) frame of reference. As in previous studies32,33, we first verified that the big lower-mantle basal structures (BLOBSs) predicted by the models were consistent with large low-shear velocity provinces (LLSVPs) inferred from 10 tomographic models and that reconstructed volcanic provinces were above or close to the mobile BLOBSs predicted by models between 320 Ma and 0 Ma (Methods and Extended Data Fig. 1). Model M1 was preferred because it predicted BLOBS areas and locations consistent with LLSVPs, and volcanic provinces close to BLOBS edges over time (Extended Data Fig. 1).

We investigated the dynamic topography predicted by these mantle flow models, which depends on the distribution of buoyancy sources and viscosity. Sources of buoyancy closer to the surface have a greater influence on the amplitude of dynamic topography, and contributions from the deep mantle are largest at the longest wavelengths34,35. We computed dynamic topography from sources of buoyancy and viscosity variations deeper than 350 km depth30, so that sources of dynamic topography nearer the surface (for example, ref. 36) were neglected. This setup resulted in smooth dynamic topography (Fig. 2a,b) at the continental scale30,37, which was desirable to test the hypothesis that the Great Unconformity could be linked to mantle flow. However, the setup is known to overpredict the amplitude of long-wavelength dynamic topography by a factor of about 2 (refs. 30,37). We therefore focused on the trend of dynamic topography evolution, which was key to our analysis, rather than its amplitude.

a,b, Dynamic topography at 640 Ma (a) and 440 Ma (b). c,d, Mantle temperature anomaly at 2,677 km depth at 640 Ma (c) and 440 Ma (d). In a–d, cyan lines represent mid-ocean ridges and transform faults, and magenta lines represent subduction zones with triangles on the overriding plate. Transparent grey polygons represent continental blocks, with labels as follows: AMZ, Amazonia; ANT, Antarctica; AUS, Australia; BAL, Baltica; CON, Congo; IND, India; KAL, Kalahari; LAU, Laurentia; NCC, North China; SF, São Francisco; SIB, Siberia; and WAC, West Africa. The green lines with diamonds are great circle transects A–A′ shown in e and f. The length of the great circle depends on its latitudinal position. Robinson projection at the surface of Earth. e,f, Cross-sections of temperature anomalies and dynamic topography across Laurentia (transect A–A′) at 640 Ma (e) and 440 Ma (f). Polar projections of longitude and depth. The colour bar in e is the temperature anomaly scale for c–f. Black arrows are velocity vectors. The amplitude of dynamic topography (not to scale) is represented above the cross-sections with positive amplitudes in red, negative amplitudes in blue, and reported values at A and A′. The black solid line indicates a depth of 2,667 km.

The motion of tectonic plates and subduction zones affected mantle convection and dynamic topography12,29,32,33,37,38 (Fig. 2 and Supplementary Videos 1 and 2). At 640 Ma, dynamic topography exhibited a north–south hemispheric planform with positive dynamic topography beneath Laurentia, Baltica, North China, Amazonia, Australia, the Kalahari Craton and Antarctica (Fig. 2a), which were above a BLOBS in the absence of subduction south of 50° S (Fig. 2c). Laurentia was tilted down to the southwest, positioned above whole-mantle upwelling (Fig. 2e). The fast motion of continental blocks and of subduction zones between 600 Ma and 320 Ma (ref. 39) reorganized mantle convection (Supplementary Videos 1 and 2) so that by 440 Ma, the hemispheric planform of dynamic topography was oriented east–west, with negative dynamic topography beneath most continental blocks, including at high latitude in both hemispheres (Fig. 2b). Laurentia was tilted down to the southeast, because of subduction-driven downwelling along its eastern margin and whole-mantle upwelling above a BLOBS in the west (Fig. 2f).

We used k-means cluster analysis to quantify the spatial and temporal evolution of continental dynamic topography during the formation (920–420 Ma) and preservation (420–0 Ma) of the Great Unconformity (Fig. 3 and Methods). We established that considering two clusters for each period was prototypical for most considered model cases except M3 and M5, for which three clusters were appropriate (Methods and Supplementary Fig. 1). These clusters, which we represented in the present-day continental configuration, captured regions in which dynamic topography evolved similarly over time (Fig. 3 and Extended Data Fig. 2).

a–c, Spatial distribution of two clusters across continental blocks that existed from 920 Ma: GU-F (Great Unconformity—formation) and GU-NF (Great Unconformity—no formation) between 920 Ma and 420 Ma (a); GU-HPP (Great Unconformity—high preservation potential) and GU-LPP (Great Unconformity—low preservation potential) from 420 Ma (b); regions in which the Great Unconformity was formed and preserved (GU-F/P), as opposed to regions with low formation and preservation potential (GU-NF/LPP) (c). Robinson projection at the surface of Earth. d,e, Temporal evolution of averaged continental dynamic topography for each cluster in a and b, respectively. The black and brown dashed lines represent the average dynamic topography for Laurentia and Baltica, respectively. The vertical dashed line represents the start of Cambrian times, and the horizontal dashed line represents the datum for dynamic topography. d, Averaged continental dynamic topography for clusters GU-F (orange) and GU-NF (grey) between 920 Ma and 420 Ma. The light-blue-shaded regions represent the duration of the two main glaciations during Cryogenian times. e, Averaged continental dynamic topography for clusters GU-HPP (orange) and GU-LPP (grey) from 420 Ma. f, Locations of orogens56 from 900 Ma (coloured by age in 100 Ma intervals). Robinson projection at the surface of Earth.

For the period 920–420 Ma, the main continental blocks in cluster GU-F (Great Unconformity—formation) were Laurentia, Baltica, northeastern North China, most of South America, Western Australia, the Kalahari Craton and parts of Antarctica. Cluster GU-NF (Great Unconformity—no formation) spanned most of Africa, Asia, parts of Antarctica and the São Francisco Craton (Fig. 3a). Cluster GU-F captured positive dynamic topography (Fig. 3d), mainly above whole-mantle upwelling (Supplementary Video 1). Dynamic topography was relatively stable between 900 Ma and 800 Ma, increased rapidly between 800 Ma and 720 Ma, followed by a gradual increase between 720 Ma and 600 Ma, and a rapid decrease between 600 Ma and 420 Ma (Fig. 3d). The predicted uplift would have promoted glacial erosion1,13 during the proposed Sturtian and Marinoan global glaciations (Fig. 3d). The GU-F pattern of prolonged dynamic uplift during Neoproterozoic times (Fig. 2 and Supplementary Videos 1 and 2), followed by dynamic subsidence during Cambrian times (Fig. 3d) was consistent across all mantle convection models (Extended Data Figs. 2 and 3a,c,e). Cluster GU-NF captured dynamic topography on average negative throughout 920–420 Ma with gradual increase between 900 Ma and 760 Ma, a rapid decline between 760 Ma and 520 Ma, and renewed increase between 520 Ma and 420 Ma (Fig. 3d). In cluster GU-NF, Siberia and the Congo and West African cratons were in a dynamic topography low surrounded by subduction zones (Fig. 2a,c and Supplementary Videos 1 and 2).

For the period 420–0 Ma, cluster GU-HPP (Great Unconformity—high preservation potential) spanned Western Laurentia, Baltica, North China and Siberia, and cluster GU-LPP (Great Unconformity—low preservation potential) spanned Eastern Laurentia, Africa, Australia, Antarctica and India (Fig. 3b). The dynamic topography for GU-HPP, which was generally negative because of subduction (Supplementary Video 1), remained relatively stable between 420 Ma and 240 Ma, before gradually declining until 0 Ma (Fig. 3e). By contrast, in GU-LPP dynamic topography increased between 420 Ma and 240 Ma, was stable between 240 Ma and 120 Ma, then gradually declined until 0 Ma (Fig. 3e).

We derived a map highlighting the areas in which the Great Unconformity was predicted to have formed and to have a high preservation potential, which consisted of Laurentia, Baltica and northeastern North China for model M1 (Fig. 3c) and included areas around Laurentia and Baltica in all six models (Extended Data Figs. 3 and 4). We analysed the sensitivity of these results to the number of clusters (either two or three) for each period (formation 920–420 Ma, preservation from 420 Ma) from vote maps (Methods) of areas in which the Great Unconformity was predicted to exist across the six models (Extended Data Fig. 5). This confirmed that Laurentia, Baltica and North China were the main continental blocks in which the Great Unconformity was predicted to have formed and to be preserved, with northern South America emerging as a possible additional region (Extended Data Fig. 5).

The dynamic topography evolution predicted by our models was consistent with the preserved sediment flux for each continent except Africa1,14 (Fig. 4 and Methods). Predicted prolonged Precambrian uplift, followed by rapid Cambrian subsidence, generally matched increased sediment flux across the Precambrian–Cambrian boundary (Fig. 4a–e). A shift from erosion to sedimentation reflecting decreasing dynamic topography (Fig. 4) and flooded continents (Extended Data Fig. 6a) was predicted for all continents except for Eurasia and Africa, which consisted of tectonic blocks with contrasting Neoproterozoic histories. In Eurasia, dynamic uplift was predicted for Baltica and North China, and dynamic subsidence for Siberia40 (Fig. 4b and Extended Data Figs. 7d and 8b,g,l,q,v,aa). In Africa, dynamic uplift was predicted for the Kalahari Craton, and dynamic subsidence for the Congo and West African cratons (Extended Data Figs. 7e and 8e,j,o,t,y,ad) was consistent with their sedimentary record of long-lived depocentres41,42. Extensive Precambrian orogens within Africa enhanced erosion and sedimentation (Fig. 3f and Extended Data Fig. 6), leading to a landscape in which negative dynamic topography did not result in increased sediment flux at the base of the Cambrian (Extended Data Fig. 6a,c,e,g).

a–e, Evolution of the preserved volume of sediment per year and per unit continental area (increasing down) (left y axis, coloured bar charts) and dynamic topography (right y axis, grey bar charts and coloured lines) for each continent averaged at time steps corresponding to the sediment preservation data1,14. Coloured solid and dotted lines represent the evolution of dynamic topography for Laurentia and continental blocks in Eurasia. f–j, Data in a–e temporally averaged for dynamic topography cycles in each continent. In each panel, the vertical dashed line represents the start of Cambrian times, and the horizontal dashed line represents the datum for dynamic topography.

The evolution of predicted Phanerozoic dynamic topography differed across continental blocks. Laurentia, Baltica and North China were characterized by sustained dynamic subsidence, which aligned with increased preserved sediment flux across North America and Eurasia (Fig. 4). Conversely, predicted renewed dynamic uplift of South America and of Australia, which would have eroded earlier unconformities11,31 and formed new ones, corresponded to decreased preserved sediment flux (Fig. 4).

Importantly, the number of dynamic topography uplift–subsidence cycles governed the formation and preservation of the Great Unconformity. A single cycle of Precambrian uplift followed by Phanerozoic subsidence was the ideal scenario for forming and preserving the Great Unconformity. This scenario, which is in first-order agreement with thermochronology studies3,4,7,10,18, was predicted for Laurentia for all models except M3 (Fig. 4a and Extended Data Fig. 8a,f,k,p,v,z). Although Laurentia was in cluster GU-F for model M3 (Extended Data Fig. 2), it was not predicted to have experienced notable uplift and was subsiding above a mantle downwelling at 640 Ma (Extended Data Fig. 9). Together with a poor match of the present-day mantle structure for M3 (Extended Data Fig. 1d), this confirmed that NNR was an appropriate reference frame to model mantle flow33, but not PMAG in which lithospheric net rotation was large. Precambrian uplift was predicted for four out of six models for Baltica and North China, with marked variations in amplitude and duration between models (Extended Data Fig. 8b,g,l,q,v,aa), possibly reflecting particularly uncertain subduction history (Supplementary Discussion and Supplementary Table 1). All models predicted dynamic uplift of Baltica as it moved from the southern hemisphere to the northern hemisphere between 540 Ma and 520 Ma (Supplementary Videos 1 and 2), followed by rapid subsidence consistent with a sub-Cambrian unconformity linked to epeirogenic uplift22,43.

By contrast, most models predicted two cycles of dynamic uplift followed by dynamic subsidence for South America and Australia and long-lived dynamic subsidence followed by dynamic uplift then renewed dynamic subsidence for Africa (Fig. 4h–j and Extended Data Fig. 8c–ad), consistent with thermochronological and geochronological evidence for these regions44,45,46,47,48. The predicted dynamic uplift of South America and Australia coincided with preserved sediment flux on these continents, as expected (Fig. 4h,i and Extended Data Fig. 8c–ac). However, the dynamic uplift of Africa coincided with increased sediment preservation because Africa was positioned centrally in Gondwana (Extended Data Fig. 6b) and orogens in Antarctica and South America (Fig. 3f) restricted drainage from Africa to the oceans, leading to endorheic (inland) sedimentation49.

The solution of the presented flow models depends strongly on the tectonic reconstruction, for which the uncertainty is large and increases back in time (Supplementary Discussion and Supplementary Table 1). Testing the sensitivity of the flow model to the tectonic scenario is a challenge that could be addressed by developing alternative tectonic reconstructions with continuously closing plate polygons or by developing a different approach to predict past mantle flow.

Comparing dynamic topography cycles to preserved sediment flux confirmed Laurentia, Baltica and North China as continental blocks on which the Great Unconformity was predicted to have formed and to be preserved (Fig. 4). The Great Unconformity surface is exposed and extensively studied in Laurentia1,3,5,6,7,9,10,15,18 and in North China8,25,26,27,28, whereas it is mostly inferred to occur beneath younger sediments in Baltica19,20,21,22,23,24. This largely stems from the tectonic and geodynamic evolution of each of these continental blocks. In the considered tectonic scenario, no subduction occurred directly along the margins of Laurentia between about 930 Ma and 510 Ma, Baltica between about 750 Ma and 520 Ma, and North China between about 720 Ma and 540 Ma (Supplementary Discussion, Supplementary Table 1 and Supplementary Videos 1 and 2). Subduction beneath northeast Laurentia from approximately 470 Ma resulted in its amalgamation with Baltica into Laurussia by around 420 Ma, associated with continent-wide Cambrian transgression (Extended Data Fig. 6a and Supplementary Videos 1 and 2). North China was on the periphery of Gondwana during Cambrian times with the Qinling subduction zone system at its western margin from 540 Ma (Fig. 2b, Supplementary Discussion, Supplementary Table 1 and Supplementary Videos 1 and 2). During the assembly of Pangea, collisions occurred along some margins of all three continental blocks (Fig. 3f and Extended Data Fig. 6b), promoting the deformation and erosion of rocks potentially preserving the Great Unconformity, or their burial in foreland basins. The large continental area of Laurentia and limited reworking at its margins were favourable to recording the formation of the continental-scale Great Unconformity. The prominent exposure of the Great Unconformity in the Grand Canyon15,16,17 has been linked to the Laramide uplift event from Farallon flat-slab subduction and subsequent Colorado River incision50,51. Repeated orogeny along the eastern margin of Baltica (Fig. 3f) could explain why the Great Unconformity is generally inferred to occur at depth on that smaller continental block. Early Cretaceous lithospheric delamination52 could explain the exposure of the Great Unconformity in North China, which is unexpected given its comparatively small area and four episodes of orogenesis between about 500 Ma and 200 Ma (Fig. 3f).

Our models predict changes in dynamic topography that when averaged in time and space by k-means clustering occur over approximately 20 Myr and about 5,000 km, suggesting that the motion of continents over the convecting mantle provided the large-scale geodynamic environments that favoured the formation and preservation of the Great Unconformity in Laurentia, Baltica and North China. The geologic record of uplift4,5,6,7,10,53 and subsidence4,5,6,7,9,10,20 indicates that the timing of erosion and deposition54 varied between locations, which probably reflects the effect of processes, such as tectonic deformation, elastic flexure or shorter wavelength dynamic topography, that would affect relative sea level over shorter spatial and temporal scales.

The amplitude of long-wavelength dynamic topography is thought to be about a tenth of the amplitude of tectonic topography37, and continental tilting would not result in the formation of slopes that would lead to sufficient fluvial erosion to explain the magnitude of denudation associated with the Great Unconformity1,4,7. We propose that sustained positive dynamic topography throughout Cryogenian times (Fig. 3d) would have resulted in substantial erosion because glacial erosion rates exceed fluvial erosion rates by an order of magnitude and can operate at lower elevations13. The rarity of extensive unconformities in the history of Earth could be due to the very long timescale (>900 Myr) of the proposed continental-scale uplift and subsidence to form such an unconformity, combined with rare extensive glaciations and decreasing preservation potential back in geological time.

Our models explain why the Great Unconformity is best preserved in North America and show that it is a first-order surface expression of deep geodynamic processes that transformed global landscapes and sediment fluxes. In turn, these landscape dynamics would have altered seawater chemistry and catalysed the Cambrian explosion of life2. Future work could investigate the effects of continental-scale dynamic uplift and subsidence on erosion, sedimentation, seawater chemistry and their consequences for the diversification of life forms.

Macrostrat is an open, relational geospatial database that enables large-scale, quantitative analysis of 33,903 lithologically and chronologically defined rock units across 1,474 regions in the Americas, New Zealand and the deep sea55.

We accessed lithostratigraphic data from the Macrostrat (https://macrostrat.org/api/units/?lith_class=sedimentary&lith_type=metasedimentary) database through theAPI (v.2). We downloaded sedimentary units and associated stratigraphic columns as GeoJSON files in June 2025. We created a map of transgressive sequences and erosional remnants across North America and northern South America (Fig. 1) spanning late Neoproterozoic to early Ordovician times.

We used the code CitcomS57 to model mantle convection for a billion years (1,000–0 Ma). In CitcomS, the mantle structure is represented with finite-element nodes in 3D spherical geometry. We considered six model cases (Extended Data Table 1), three of which have been presented in previous work (M4 was MF in ref. 58; M5 was C3 in ref. 59, C20 in ref. 33 and C3 in ref. 60; and M6 was C1 in ref. 59).

We discretized the mantle into about 13 million nodes (129 × 129 × 65 × 12), with radial mesh refinements at the surface (about 50 × 50 × 15 km) and core–mantle boundary (CMB; about 28 × 28 × 27 km) and relatively lower resolution in the mid-mantle (approximately 40 × 40 × 100 km). We reconstructed mantle flow in a modified version of CitcomS57,61 in which plate kinematics and the thermal structure of the oceanic lithosphere and subducting slabs down to 350 km depth were derived from tectonic reconstructions62 with continuously closing plate polygons63 and imposed as time-dependent boundary conditions in 1 million-year increments. We used the extended Boussinesq approximation that assumed the mantle to be an incompressible fluid to account for viscous dissipation, internal heating, depth-dependent thermal expansion coefficient and an adiabatic temperature gradient64.

For initial boundary conditions and time-progressive model simulation, we created a lithospheric thermal structure from reconstructed seafloor ages and half-space cooling with a maximum seafloor age set as 80 Myr to obtain a maximum thickness of oceanic lithosphere consistent with observations for the present day. We used the method in ref. 65 to reconstruct synthetic seafloor ages, whereas the continental lithosphere adopted simplified tectonothermal ages from ref. 66. The global thermal regime of continental lithosphere and subducting slabs, reconstructed using seafloor ages and location of subduction zones61, was imposed in the flow models in increments of 1 million years.

The initial conditions included an adiabatic temperature profile between two boundary layers: the lithosphere at the surface, and a 225 km thick laterally uniform basal layer containing a 113 km thick layer with excess density. The density contrast δρb between the basal layer and the ambient mantle was defined by the buoyancy ratio \(B=\frac{{\rm{\delta }}{\rho }_{{\rm{b}}}}{\rho \alpha \Delta T}\) where ΔT = 4,300 K was the temperature change across mantle for M1–M3 (ΔT = 3,600 K for M4 and ΔT = 2,800 K for M5 and M6), ρ = 5,546 kg m−3 was the average density67 and α = 1.32 × 10−5 K−1 was thermal expansivity68 in the 100 km layer above the CMB. The initial condition consisted of slabs inserted down to 1,000 km depth for models M1–M4 (1,200 km for models M5 and 550 km for M6) with dip angles of 45° dip down to 425 km depth and 90° descent below. To incorporate the advective thickening of more viscous lower mantle, lower mantle slabs were twice as thick as upper mantle slabs in the initial condition. Models were initialized with differing warm-up phases lasting 250 Myr for models M1 and M4, 200 Myr for models M6 and 0 Myr for other models (Extended Data Table 1) using the 1 Ga configuration for tectonic velocities, subduction zone positions and lithospheric age. Boundary conditions were isothermal at the surface and at the CMB, imposed plate kinematics (velocities) at the surface and a free-slip kinematic condition at the CMB.

The convective vigour in models was governed by the Rayleigh number \({\rm{R}}{\rm{a}}=\frac{{\alpha }_{0}\rho g\Delta T{h}_{{\rm{M}}}^{3}}{\kappa {\eta }_{0}}\), where α0 = 3 × 10−5 K−1 was the coefficient of thermal expansion at the surface, ρ = 4,000 kg m−3 was the density, g = 9.81 m s−2 was the gravitational acceleration, hM = 2,867 km was the thickness of the mantle, κ = 1 × 10−6 m2 s−1 was the thermal diffusivity, η0 = 1 × 1021 Pa s was the reference viscosity. The subscript ‘0’ indicated reference values. The coefficient of thermal expansion was depth-dependent, decreasing by a factor of about 2 over the thickness of the mantle (see refs. 68,69). Based on these values, we obtained Ra = 1.2 × 108 for M1–M3. The Rayleigh number was varied across model cases (Extended Data Table 1).

Likewise, the dissipation number governed heat dissipation generated by shear heating. It was given by \({\rm{D}}{\rm{i}}=\frac{{\alpha }_{0}g{h}_{{\rm{M}}}}{{C}_{p}}\), where 2867 Cp = 1,200 J kg−1 K−1 was the heat capacity. The total rate of internal heating was equal to 33.6 TW, accounting for contributions from both radioactive decay (about 9–17 TW; ref. 70) and primordial heat dissipated through secular cooling of the interior of Earth (around 8–29 TW; ref. 70).

Depth-, composition-, temperature- and pressure-dependent viscosity was computed as

The depth-dependent viscosity pre-factor η(r) was equal to 2 × 1019 Pa s above 160 km depth and between 310 km and 660 km depth (upper mantle), to 6 × 1017 Pa s in the asthenosphere between 60 km and 310 km depth for models M1–M3 (2 × 1018 Pa s for models M4–M6), and 6 × 1020 Pa s in the lower mantle below 660 km depth for models M1–M3 (2 × 1020 Pa s for models M4–M6; Extended Data Table 1). The compositional viscosity pre-factors ηC were equal to 1 for ambient mantle, to 100 for continental lithosphere (modelled as in ref. 66), and to 10 for the basal layer. The term r was the radius, Rc = 3,504 km was the radius of the core, Eη = 284 kJ mol−1 was the activation energy, Zη = 2.1 × 10−6 m3 mol−1 was the activation volume, Ru = 8.31 J mol−1 K−1 was the universal gas constant, T was the dimensional temperature, Toff = 694 K was a temperature offset and TCMB = 4,300 K was the temperature at the core–mantle boundary. The viscosity structure, defined by the viscosity pre-factors, activation volume, activation energy and temperature offset produced viscosity variations varying over three orders of magnitude across the model33. Although these contrasts were smaller than expected for the solid Earth71, these lateral viscosity variations could be resolved at a spatial resolution that allows time-dependent mantle flow to be computed using up to about 15,000 CPU hours per 100 million years on supercomputer Gadi.

We derived boundary conditions from the global tectonic reconstructions in ref. 62 (which merges with tectonic reconstructions in refs. 72,73,74,75), which was the only tectonic reconstruction extending back to 1 billion years ago with continuously closing plate polygons that are necessary in models based on the approach in ref. 61. We considered two reference frames for the tectonic reconstruction in ref. 62: the original palaeomagnetic reference frame (PMAG, model M3) and a no-net-rotation reference frame (NNR), which was suitable to model mantle convection33,76. We analysed model results, including dynamic topography, mantle temperature and composition fields in increments of 20 million years.

We computed air-loaded dynamic topography at the surface of Earth as \(h=\frac{{\sigma }_{\mathrm{rr}}}{\Delta \rho g}\), where g = 9.81 m s−2 was the acceleration of gravity and Δρ was the difference in densities between air (ρA = 0 kg m−3) and the shallow upper mantle (ρUM = 3,320 kg m−3). We considered free-slip boundary conditions, contributions from sources of buoyancy deeper than 350 km depth, and lateral viscosity variations deeper than 350 km depth.

As in refs. 32,33,77, we first classified the present-day lower mantle structure as mapped by 10 independent S-wave tomographic models78,79,80,81,82,83,84,85,86,87 and predicted by six mantle flow models (M1–M6). To achieve this, we generated 196,965 evenly spaced points (about 0.45°) on the surface and sampled mantle temperature (seismic velocity) approximately every 58 km between 1,000 km and 2,800 km depths. We then used k-means88 clustering to group these points into user-specified k clusters such that the within-cluster sum of squares (WCSS), that is, the squared Euclidean distances between points and the centroid of the group was minimized.

As in previous studies32,33, we examined model success by computing three metrics (Extended Data Fig. 1): (1) the predicted fractional area fa of the surface of Earth covered by clusters for hot BLOBSs (for mantle flow models) and slow LLSVPs (for tomographic models), (2) the global accuracy (\(\overline{\mathrm{Acc}}\)), which was a measure of the spatial match between the present-day mantle structure (clusters) predicted by mantle convection models and that averaged across 10 independent tomographic models given by \(\overline{\mathrm{Acc}}=\frac{\mathrm{TP}+\mathrm{TN}}{A}\), where TP was the area of true positives representing spatial match between hot BLOBSs and LLSVPs, TN the area of the true negatives measuring the spatial extent of cold basal mantle structure and high seismic velocity profiles and A was the total surface area of Earth. For each model, the mean accuracy \(\overline{\mathrm{Acc}}\) represented the average across 10 tomographic models, whereas for each tomographic model, \(\overline{\mathrm{Acc}}\) was computed as an average across the nine independent tomographic models; and (3) the time-averaged median angular distance \(\widetilde{\theta }\) between reconstructed volcanic eruption locations (LIPs and kimberlites as in ref. 33) from 320 Ma and the edge of hot BLOBSs. The distance was taken as zero for eruption locations above a BLOBS or LLSVP. Smaller distances indicated a close spatial match between BLOBSs or LLSVPs and volcanic eruptions, which was thought to be favourable32,33,89. Mantle flow models were deemed to perform better if all three metrics were within the range or close to the range for tomographic models (Extended Data Fig. 1, grey areas).

We generated a set of evenly spaced (about 0.45°) points entirely covering present-day continents. We extracted dynamic topography at the reconstructed location of these points in 20 Myr intervals and rotated the results back into the present-day plate configuration. We used the continental blocks that continuously existed from 920 Ma to mask data for all other times so that the considered locations existed for all considered times. We used k-means clustering88 as in ref. 90 to classify geographic regions that share a similar evolution of predicted dynamic topography.

We used the silhouette91 score, Davies–Bouldin index92 (DBI) and elbow method93to determine the appropriate number of clusters to consider (Supplementary Fig. 1). The silhouette score measured how similar a point was to its own cluster compared with other clusters. It combined intra-cluster cohesion and inter-cluster separation. Silhouette scores ranged from −1 to 1, with larger values indicating better-defined clusters. The DBI evaluated intra-cluster similarity and inter-cluster differences based on intra-cluster dispersion and inter-cluster distance. Lower scores indicated better clustering. It was computationally efficient but assumed compact, spherical clusters, making it less reliable for irregular shapes. The heuristic elbow method consisted of plotting the number of clusters (k) against the clustering cost (for example, WCSS) and identifying the ‘elbow’ point, at which the rate of improvement (decrease in WCSS) decreased sharply, suggesting the most appropriate k.

We identified the ideal number of clusters for all six model cases for both the Great Unconformity formation (920–420 Ma) and preservation (420–0 Ma) periods to be equal to either two or three (Supplementary Fig. 1). We produced cluster maps for each model case and each cluster combination (either two or three) and combined them in maps indicating model agreement with a score between zero and six out of six models. These ‘vote’ maps highlighted regions showing both formation and preservation of the Great Unconformity across model and cluster combinations (Extended Data Fig. 5).

We obtained the preserved sediment flux (sediment volume divided by time) from Neoproterozoic times (1.6 Ga) to the present for North America, South America, Africa, Eurasia and Australia from ref. 1. For the period 920–0 Ma, we scaled sediment flux by the present-day area of each considered continent as in ref. 1. We averaged continental dynamic topography for each continental block that continuously existed between 920 Ma and 0 Ma (Extended Data Fig. 8a) using the time periods at which sediment volume data were defined (Fig. 4a and Extended Data Figs. 7 and 8).

To focus on long-term, long-wavelength processes, we filtered the preserved sediment data using time windows that corresponded to the periods of dynamic uplift and dynamic subsidence predicted for each continent. We then averaged the preserved sediment volume to represent the sediment accumulation associated with each phase of dynamic topography (Fig. 4f–j).

The subduction convergence rates at trench segments were computed using plate-kinematic workflow of GPlately (v.2.0.0), built atop PyGPlates94, a Python interface for GPlates95 and PlateTectonicTools. The process consisted of resolving the topological plate model and extracting subduction zones from the network of dynamic plate boundaries reconstructed at a specified age using the NNR model. Each subduction zone was then tessellated, that is, discretized into a series of evenly spaced points using the ‘tessellation_subduction_zone’ module in GPlately. At each tessellated point, subduction convergence rate, obliquity and trench migration rate were calculated from the relative motion of the down-going and overriding plates at each reconstruction time step. Negative convergence-rate values, which indicated infrequent inconsistencies in the model with divergence occurring at a convergent boundary72, were set to zero before computing the range of convergence rates for each subduction zone listed in Supplementary Table 1.

#1337. Carrick’s United are in crisis and now spotlight is on Wilcox

Michael Carrick had urged his Manchester United players to come out and fight. But nobody could have imagined quite how Lisandro Martínez would interpret that message.

By the end of an extraordinary evening in Madrid, where United went 1-0 down inside a minute and never recovered against Atlético Madrid, Martínez had blown the lid off any pretence of all being well at the club as he launched a lacerating assault on the club’s executives.

United had come into this getting battered from all sides and when Pablo Barrios put Atlético ahead, Jamie Carragher’s pre-match assessment about how things could get “very messy, very quickly” for all involved at Old Trafford must have been ringing in the ears of the travelling supporters.

ATLETICO ARE AHEAD IN JUST 53 SECONDS! ⚡️ A nightmare start for United at the Metropolitano Stadium 😬 https://t.co/TdOwoXxopn

They certainly know how to make life difficult for themselves. Leny Yoro’s 74th-minute red card pretty much ended hopes of them taking something from the game.

Ademola Lookman scored Atlético’s second soon after and Carrick was staring at another defeat. And so they now move on to a big game at Leeds on Sunday. This was not the result Carrick would have wanted – and that is before what happened off the pitch.

Ademola Lookman PUNISHES a 10-man Man United 💥 https://t.co/GHKYIHGhNC

Another defeat intensified the pressure on Carrick but Martínez left nobody under any illusions that he felt the finger should be pointed not simply at another manager or the players, but the hierarchy above him.

It was extraordinary to see a player speaking out so publicly in this fashion against his own bosses.

But Martínez pulled no punches, even going as far as singling out Jason Wilcox, the director of football, as he criticised the club’s summer transfer business and effectively accused the club of failing Carrick and the players in the window.

To what extent Martínez’s comments mirror the views of the wider dressing room is unclear, but you have to wonder where Carrick and United go from here.

On the one hand, Martínez was providing a show of support for his manager by attacking the people above him. At the same time, he has presented Carrick with a disciplinary problem to address.

Lisandro Martínez did NOT hold back after United's loss to Atletico 😬👀 https://t.co/OGo25Pzd30

And United have enough troubles as it is without a senior member of Carrick’s dressing room turning so squarely against the club’s power brokers.

Martínez was probably only giving voice to what many fans have been saying since an underwhelming transfer window closed with more questions than answers. But for a player to talk in such blunt, excoriating terms resonated more loudly than anything a supporter or United’s most caustic critic could say.

The message was simple: you can sack all the managers you want but until you pull together a squad worthy of United’s name and give the man at the helm the tools to compete, the club will struggle to escape this cycle of mediocrity.

No one can reasonably argue United’s window was a success. They went into it with the hopes of landing Elliot Anderson and other premium midfielders but ended up going for numbers over proven quality or pedigree. Youri Tielemans, Andrey Santos and Carlos Baleba were not a trio of signings anyone expected at the start of summer, not even the club itself.

There were glaring issues to address in defence, not least at left-back, and at centre-forward but a quality alternative to Luke Shaw never materialised and no back-up was signed for Benjamin Sesko, who was missing for four months with a shin injury that has since resurfaced and which could keep him out for a while yet.

Having done so well to lead United to third and take them back into the Champions League, Carrick would have expected further backing than he got in the summer. Ever the company man, he has been too polite to criticise that lack of investment. But the cat is out of the bag now Martínez has had his say.

It now places the spotlight on Wilcox. United head to Elland Road on Sunday and that was the scene of Rúben Amorim’s final meltdown as manager. Two days after he blew up in a meeting with Wilcox at United’s Carrington training base, Amorim took aim at the director of football and others at the club, demanding they “do their job” and repeatedly declaring that he had come to Old Trafford to “be the manager, not to be the coach”.

It is remarkable to think that, 10 months on, United head back to Leeds with just as many questions as there were back then.

United’s worst start to a league season for 40 years has ensured Carrick is already under pressure, but Martínez is very much of the view that it is no longer enough for the manager and the players to keep carrying the can and that the credibility and suitability of those who recruit the players and make the decisions must now be called into question.

That Martínez picked this game to speak out was interesting. United, lost, yes, and the manner of Atlético’s opening goal from Barrios after 53 seconds was shocking. But United at least went down fighting on this occasion and had fashioned enough good chances to at least draw level before Yoro’s harsh 74th-minute red card swung a delicately poised match decisively in Atlético’s favour.

Lookman made it 2-0 soon after, but Atlético, having looked like they would run all over United in those opening 10 minutes, were made to work hard for their victory.

United cannot keep shooting themselves in the foot like they did in the first minute. Carrick had gone with a three-man midfield to shore things up and made his team more comfortable and yet they were opened up in double quick time by two passes through the middle.

Still, you only needed to look across at United’s opponents to appreciate how chaotic it had become at Old Trafford.

Diego Simeone’s reign at Atlético covers a period stretching two years longer than the post-Ferguson era and in many ways his teams have represented everything United have not been in that time: well constructed and thought through, unified, stable, organised, hungry, aggressive, uncompromising and with a flash of devilment.

If United were not in crisis before this, they are now.

Lisandro Martínez did NOT hold back after United's loss to Atletico 😬👀 https://t.co/OGo25Pzd30

[The performance] was a little bit mixed. It’s a tough enough place to come and the start we had put us in a difficult situation. I thought we grew into the game, had four big chances and [score one or more] and the game looks really different. They were really good chances.

And then the red card which I thought was a really poor one. It’s difficult after that. Disappointed that with the chances we had we didn’t [get] more [out of the game].

I haven’t seen [Martinez’s interview]. After a game like this you come here to try and get something from the game and you are disappointed and can be a little bit emotional. I have not seen it so I don’t think it is the right time for me to comment on it.

I fully know we all care and show that in different ways but now is the time to be together and work through. We have a big game on Sunday.

[What do you make of Lisandro’s comments?] I have no comment about that.

The only thing that’s going to get us back into it is to get a few wins.

It is very hard to say after a defeat that there are positives. We just have to work hard to keep working and keep trusting in our structure.

We have to keep working, keep trusting each other and be together on this.

I always wanted to be outspoken as a player but I think he’s gone too far. You can clearly see he cares and wants the club to invest more in new players but his performances have not been good enough. In some ways he’s right, the club needs to invest more. It looks like a bit of an agenda because it wasn’t a poor performance.

[How do you sum up the performance?] Really poor, Really poor. I have to control myself a lot. Sometimes it’s a mirror of the reflection of how our club is. We had a fantastic season last season but in order to compete we needed to buy more players. Many teams buy many players and Atletico Madrid did. They have an amazing team and deserved to win today.

I expected more. [Are you saying you expected more investment in the squad this summer?] Yes 100 per cent. I expect more from our technical director. I have to be honest. As players we have to do more but it is important to make a strong squad to be ready for for this kind of night.

In general, in general [should you have invested more in defence and attack given all the midfielders]. Last season we made a strong base to build an amazing team. It’s annoying and disappointing coming here and trying to get a result.

I don’t think so [was the manager backed?] He does his best. You can’t [live on] what you did last season. Every season is different. You can’t stay with what you did last season. The teams knows how you play, they know every detail, if you don’t change next season is a big problem.

It’s changing, changing, changing the manager [after a poor run]. But what about other areas? I can’t say more.

Tonight is it easy to say the coach, easy to say the players [are at fault]. But we have to look at other areas.

So far this season there have been more times when the performances have been worse than the results. This was the other way round but there is a sizeable quality gap between Carrick’s squad and the company they are keeping. They can point to a soft red card but they still shot themselves in the foot with their doziness in the first minute and squandering the good chances they created.

Maguire strays offside when Mount, from the short corner, tries to pick him out at the back post.

Amad, now on the right, tries to dribble past Grimaldo who wins the ball off him but Atletico give it straight back. Man Utd work it into the box for Zirkzee to cushion and then dither so long over a shot he has to lay it off to Cunha who hits it straight at the keeper with two-thirds of the goal vacant. Oblak turns it wide.

Five minutes of stoppage time are signalled.

Alan Shearer says there has been improvement tonight since Saturday. “They have stuck together and have not been outrun.” This is a very low bar but OK. He goes on to say that the glaring weakness is not attitude but a lack of finishing quality.

And Le Normand is booked within seconds of his introduction for a tug of the shirt.

Dalot lofts a deep cross way beyond Zirkzee. I think Dalot encompasses Man Utd’s recruitment over the past eight years or so in that it’s hard to see any progression or improvement since the day they signed him. Maybe he always had a low ceiling. But where on earth is the coaching?

Manchester United have had their chances but they have lacked an elite or even merely decent finisher.

Atletico 2 Man Utd 0 (Lookman)  The three men were not enough and were carved apart by one pass from the left, from Grimaldo I think to David who opened his body to fire a shot towards the bottom right. Lammens dives to save but Lookman is Johnny on the spot to beat Dalot to the rebound and score.

Carrick now has three at the back after the sending off.

He places his hand on his shoulder and let it creep down on to Lookman’s chest as the former Everton winger tried to run clear from 40 yards.

The referee is sent to the screen to look again at Yoro’s contact on Lookman, the hand on the shoulder. Was it DOGSO, denial of a goalscoring opportunity. It was very weak.

Fernandes plays the corner to Amad standing to the left of the D, who rolls it halfway back and the captain wraps his foot around a blistering shot that thumps into the crossbar.

Cute pass from Heaven sends Amad down the left but still no target for him to find and he has to settle for a corner.

Mount wins the ball off Baena, passes out to Dalot on the right and he squares it to Bruno Fernandes. The captain opens his foot to shoot and the ball deflects off Zirkzee, killing its power. Oblak flops forward to gather.

Amad is on the left, Mbeumo to the right and Zirkzee down the middle with Fernandes tucked behind.

After Baena shoots at Lammens, Man Utd make a triple substitution:

Amad → RashfordMount → BalebaZirkzee → Tielemans.

Cross from the right. Bruno whips it around the left-back but Mbeumo, not really a centre-forward, held his line rather than running across Romero’s shoulder and that allows the former Spurs captain to get there first. Bruno signals his frustration.

Pubill goes to right-back and Llorente moves into midfield.

Baena cuts in off the left to shoot with his right, trying to curl it into the top right but the ball will not bend to his will and ends up being far to straight. He was looking for a banana bend and ended up with a cucumber.

Manchester United carve Atletico open with a simple long, left to right diagonal pass that Romero misjudges. Fernandes leaps to try to hook it on the volley over Oblak but instead steers it wide of the left post.

Terrific pass from Barrios picks out Alvarez on the left of the box and he thumps his shot into the post. Lammens, who dived to try to stop it, is stranded but Martinez is there to scramble the ball behind as it rebounded into the six-yard box.

Rashford slips Tielemans down the left and he stands up a cross that Oblan can pick out of the sky unmolested. Might be worth a gamble if they had Sesko to bring on.

Baena arrows a long cross straight at Lammens.

Good work from Baleba to win the ball off Barrios as the arrowhead of a three-man press but his chip down the left finds Rashford offside.

A foul on Fernandes is followed 40 seconds later by Rashford being penalised for trying to get past Simeone by holding his shoulder.

Yoro pushes high into the press and dispossesses Grimaldo and squares it to Bruno Fernandes. He clips a pass towards the penalty spot but too far from Mbeumo. Fernandes is patently unfit. I know he’s the captain/talisman but he is not very effective tonight.

No doubt Manchester United have improved and created a couple of chances for Mbeumo and one for Rashford. Baleba should really have buried that free back-post header from the corner, too. And that second Atletico ‘goal’ being disallowed was a real tonic on the stroke of half-time. Kudos fro not crumbling. But I wouldn’t be surprised if Baena, Alvarez and Lee carved them open again.

Tielemans is penalised for a foul on Cardoso who has no time to do anything with the free-kick in his own half.

The ball hit Llorente’s hand as it bounced back off Heaven in a block tackle before Cardoso swept a right-foot shot into the bottom left.

No goal! He gained an advantage and the referee chalks it off.

Alvarez picks up his head and spanks a right-foot shot from 25 yards over the bar.

The home crowd gasps as Baena traps a 40-yard crossfield chip on his thigh and fizzes a pass inside to Alvarez who gives it right back to him but Yoro had stuck with him and stops the danger.

This feels a big moment for Carrick and United’s players to answer some of their critics. They have been getting battered from all sides in the last couple of days. Nicky Butt suggested on his podcast that Carrick told him before he got the United job that management “not for me” and “my head’s all over the shop” and that United was the only job he would take. At the very least, those comments are unhelpful and they are thought to have been dimly received internally.

Jamie Carragher offered a lacerating analysis of United’s performance against Spurs on Saturday on Sky Sports on Monday night and suggested things could get “very messy, very quickly” for all involved if there is not marked improvement. Steven Gerrard questioned why United opted to invest £50m of their summer budget in Andrey Santos, an unused substitute in the last three league games, insisted the back four was not good enough and questioned the work ethic.

And it was interesting to see Carrick alongside his mate Wayne Rooney just now pitchside. Rooney told the Stick to United podcast that captain Bruno Fernandes looks “fed up” and ready to explode at any moment.

It would have been pretty unthinkable for Carrick not to run with a three-man midfield here, not just because of the wide open spaces opponents have exploited this season but when you look at the back line United are fielding. Dalot at left back, two youngsters in Lenny Yoro and Ayden Heaven and a horribly out of form Lisandro Maríinez.

Nor has Senne Lammens looked convincing this term. Matheus Cunha has been dropped – not before time – and I expect to see Fernandes playing off the right. There’s going to a big onus on Rashford on the left. I’m not sure if he is fully fit but he’s going to be important.

It’s fantastic. It’s where we want to be, these games, these competitions. It’s as tough a place as you can come to. They’ve got a really good history in this competition and it’s where we want to come to challenge and test ourselves. We have put ourselves in this position, got a good start at home and now this is our first away game.

We want a reaction, of course. A positive reaction [to Saturday’s poor performance]. It hasn’t gone how we wanted, how we expected so far but it’s been fine margins in some of those games. It can go both ways but the reality is where we are at now.

It’s a fresh night and we’ve got to adapt, we’ve got to adjust in a positive way.

We want a little more control in the game [with three central midfielders]. At times we have been too open. We wanted to make a difference in that way. We’ve made other changes, certain spaces, certain positions.

To be honest it’s not really a big change of shape, personnel maybe but a lot of it is similar. We want more control, a little bit without the ball and a lot more with it. We’re happy with the way we set up.

Look at the last three goals we’ve conceded. They’re a mixed bag, simple goals you can something about. We need to defend better as a whole team .

Good evening and welcome to live coverage of the Champions League tie between Atlético Madrid and Manchester United from the Metropolitano. The two sides had contrasting fortunes in their opening fixtures in this competition, Man Utd beating Azerbaijan’s Sabah 4-0 at Old Trafford a month ago while Atléti were defeated by Liverpool who came back from 1-0 down to win 2-1.

But domestically it is the other way round – Michael Carrick’s side have made the club’s worst start in the league for 40 years with one win, three draws and two defeats and have been knocked out of the League Cup. Those of us who watch them regularly – purely because of occupational obligations in this instance – have been surprised by how poor they have been. The results have been bad but the performances even worse.

They seem to lack players who can play on the front foot, who have the athletic dynamism required in this league and too many self-indulgent forward players who either can’t be bothered to help out their team-mates or cannot concentrate long enough to do so. Spooked by their lack of pace in defence and midfield, they are hidebound by caution, dropping ever deeper, ever more reliant on counter-attacking despite the blatant disconnect between the front four and back six. If they drift through this match and Sunday’s trip to Elland Road, Carrick may join the long list of Ineos-driven managerial mis-steps.

Atlético have won six of eight in La Liga and have been defeated only once. They are five points behind Barcelona in second and have score 18 goals and let in eight, which may seem a curious thing to include in a preview but it is done to emphasise that many fans’ perception of Diego Simeone’s team are out of date. Back in the days of Diego Godín, Gabi, Juanfran et all, six wins a draw and a defeat would have had goals for of about 10 and goals against of maybe three.

Simeone is a martinet about attitude not systems or styles and his team have evolved, with the World Cup-winner Alex Baena, who has scored four goals so far, driving them on. He has reintegrated Julián Alvarez, too, after his brazen attempt to force a move to Barcelona so incensed Atléti fans that it seemed they would drive him out of the club. Simeone refused to let Alvarez get his own way and he is now buckling down. Ten years ago Simeone would have bitten his head off.

The one surviving veteran in the squad from that first of El Cholo’s Liga winning sides and the two Champions League finals, victory in which would represent Simeone’s crowning achievement, is the midfielder Koke. Remarkably, if he features today, the 34-year-old midfielder will be making his 750th first-team appearance as an Atlético player.

Barcelona are reportedly interested in signing Arsenal defender Piero Hincapie as Deco looks to strengthen Hansi Flick’s defensive options ahead of the January transfer window.

According to a report from Sport, the Catalan giants have identified the Ecuadorian international as a potential defensive addition, with the club’s sporting director already exploring the possibility of bringing him to Camp Nou.

Barcelona are keen to add more quality and depth to their defensive unit, and Hincapie could be an attractive option for the Spanish giants. The 24-year-old has struggled to establish himself as a regular starter at Arsenal this season, which could potentially open the door for a January departure.

The Ecuadorian international has several qualities that make him an appealing target for Flick. He is naturally left-footed and comfortable operating both as a centre-back and left-back, offering the German manager valuable tactical flexibility.

Hincapie also has considerable experience at the highest level, having previously impressed during his time at Bayer Leverkusen before moving to the Premier League.

Reports suggest Deco and Flick have received positive assessments of the defender, with the Barcelona sporting director reportedly making initial contact with his representatives to understand his willingness to consider a move.

Mikel Arteta remains reluctant to weaken his squad during the January transfer window, particularly with the Gunners competing across multiple competitions. Despite the defender’s limited involvement this season, the Spanish manager may be unwilling to sanction his departure.

Barcelona will therefore need to assess their options carefully before making a formal approach. Hincapie’s versatility and potential make him an interesting addition, but Arsenal’s stance could ultimately determine whether the Catalan giants can turn their reported interest into a concrete transfer.

#1335. Forget Hassan: O'Neill Must Drop Carter-Vickers for Celtic vs Besiktas

Celtic are looking to bounce back from the disappointing defeat to Falkirk as they aim to avoid a fourth successive Europa League loss against Besiktas at Parkhead on Thursday night.

Celtic's second league defeat of the season came in shocking circumstances as Falkirk beat them for the first time in 19 years, with the Bairns' last victory against the Hoops coming in 2007.

The Bhoys remain four points clear at the summit of the Scottish Premiership, although second-place Rangers do have a game in hand on their Old Firm rivals.

Martin O'Neill was understandably disappointed with the result on Sunday, which followed the 2-2 draw at home to Dundee United.

While their league form has generally been pretty good, it's been a different story in Europe.

Celtic have lost all three of their Europa League matches against Ferencvaros, Benfica and Celta Vigo, with the clashes against the Hungarian and Spanish sides being at their Celtic Park home.

Next up for O'Neill's men is another home tie against Turkish giants Besiktas, with the Glasgow outfit currently lying second bottom of the 36-team table.

There was a lot to be unimpressed with from the loss to Falkirk, and the veteran Northern Irish manager may well be considering making some changes against Besiktas as they look to pick up their first points of the campaign.

Haissem Hassan's place could be under threat, even though O'Neill has admitted that the Egyptian winger could have a better output had chances not been squandered by his teammates in the opening months of the campaign.

Still, the £6m signing has no goals and two assists in his first 16 appearances for Celtic, and that number needs to increase if he is to justify a spot in the starting XI.

The 24-year-old's place in the team on Thursday shouldn't be the only one under threat though.

The jury is still out on whether the centre-back partnership of Liam Scales and Dane Murray is good enough to be starting consistently for Celtic.

O'Neill decided after the 2-2 draw with Dundee United that he was going to reunite the title-winning partnership of Scales and Cameron Carter-Vickers against Falkirk, but it was a decision that didn't pay off.

Celtic were beaten 2-0 and while the two centre-backs weren't the only poor performers on the day, they came away from the game with little praise.

It's only been six weeks since Carter-Vickers came out and criticised the team's lack of identity following the 1-0 home defeat to Rangers, as he appeared to hit out at O'Neill's tactics.

The 28-year-old had the perfect opportunity to do his talking on the pitch against Falkirk, but instead he was handed a 2/10 rating by 67 Hail Hail for his performance.

The Englishman was given the worst rating of any Hoops player, and it was described as one of his worst games in his 185 appearances in a Celtic shirt.

Former Celtic striker Chris Sutton has questioned defender Cameron Carter-Vickers after his recent displays.

He repeatedly made errors against Falkirk, and all it showed was that the club needs to invest in the centre-back position in 2027 if they want to improve.

O'Neill now has a decision to make on the Carter-Vickers and Scales partnership ahead of the visit of Besiktas, and the temptation might be to go with experience over Murray.

However, the 74-year-old manager should give Murray another chance against the Turkish outfit to see if he can have a long-term future at Parkhead, in a competition from which they will already struggle to qualify for the next stage.

#1334. Barcola starts to justify £123m price tag with hat-trick as Liverpool hit LASK for six

There was no grand gesture as Bradley Barcola walked back to the bench, just a high-five from Andoni Iraola and some of Liverpool’s coaching staff.

It was a similar situation as he left the stadium. Hood up, jacket zipped, baseball cap pulled on tightly, he politely turned down all requests to talk in English. “Not good enough,” he said with a smile, but that was the only thing that had not been up to standard.

The giveaway here was what he held in his right hand – the match ball. On it were the signatures of Liverpool’s squad, congratulating him on a momentous performance that had arrived right on cue.

If you are going end a barren spell, you do not want to just turn on the taps but burst the dam, and that is precisely what Barcola did on a wild night in Austria. He needed one goal to get his Liverpool career up and running, he ended up scoring three.

Iraola had said he was not concerned about Barcola’s numbers when Liverpool arrived in Linz, even if no goals and no assists since his £123m move from Paris St-Germain had caused debate, but those numbers look infinitely better now after his first senior hat-trick.

Bradley Barcola's first ever senior hat-trick ⚽️ He's been unplayable 🔥 📺 Stream now on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/UMhUDmGPo9

“I’m really happy for Bradley, because you were asking me yesterday about him, not making the numbers,” Iraola smiled. “Also Florian [Wirtz], and I think both of them played really, really well. They made a difference. Bradley apart from the hat-trick I thought he was a threat.

“He was always one-on-one, certainly in behind and he helped us a lot to control the game, finding the pockets. I am happy for both of them, yes. For their confidence for sure, it’s very good. I think they feel now that we trust them a lot. It’s going to be very good for them.”

Barcola should have had the stage to himself on an evening when Liverpool were so obviously better than LASK in Linz but it will have frustrated Iraola immensely that his team scoring six times was tarnished by three daft goals being given up in the final 25 minutes.

19 - Liverpool have recorded the most shots by an away team on record in the first half of a UEFA Champions League away match (since 2003-04). Volume. https://t.co/AFlsqZlKFh

Liverpool well on their way to consecutive wins in the Champions League league phase, and the big positive is the threat offered by Barcola, Wirtz as well as Ngumoha. Barcola and Wirtz also offered signs of a promising partnership. The gulf in class is stark, and Iraola can now make changes with Brentford in mind.

Wirtz looking a far more confident player, not that this is the most exacting test, and he tests the goalkeeper with a curling shot towards the far corner. There will be just one minute of added time to play.

Liverpool’s wingers Barcola and Ngumoha have just been far to sharp for their markers, LASK cannot cope with the pace on offer. The home team keep pushing numbers forward which could be a dangerous straregy.

That’s a very nifty assist from Florian Wirtz, played through legs into Barcola’s feet in the box, and the French winger’s touch teed him up for a left-footed finish across the goalkeeper. Game over, which was already the case.

What a difference a goal makes. Barcola’s touches and feints and skills are getting a full airing now and rightly so. He looks like he is relaxing and he should be aiming to score himself a hat-trick. Liverpool are miles clear of this team.

Writing Partnership building... 👀 Florian Wirtz and Bradley Barcola link up for Liverpool's third 🔥 📺 Stream now on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/AffQ8kSy2C

This game is a non-contest. Gravenberch lines up another shot from the edge of the box, before Barcola shows some quick feet in the box and his side-footed attempt loops over. The question for Iraola is the extent to which these performances and chances created will translate to Premier League standard.

Ryan Gravenberch so unlucky not to score with a shot across Jungwirth, which struck the inside of the far post and bounced away to safety, before a Wirtz shot deflects behind. Liverpool waltzing through the LASK defence with ease now.

Lewis Koumas thought he had scored a third for Liverpool, but the flag was raised for offside. He was a yard or two off, but it was still a very accomplished finish.

Liverpool just need a goal or two from Wirtz now and the night would be complete. LASK actually made a confident start in the first 20 minutes but conceding from a corner has deflated them.

Barcola is the scorer, but the initial danger was instigated by Ngumoha, dribbling around the outside of the LASK defence and into the box where he is tackled. The ball breaks free to Koumas, and he sets it back for Barcola to find the far corner. Liverpool now in command.

The goals have been coming from Liverpool and, really, it should be a night for them to plunder a hatful. LASK have loud supporters and the atmosphere being created is typically of one of these smaller European stadiums but Liverpool are miles better than LASK and should rip them apart. Bradley Barcola looked like a weight had been lifted as he got his first goal and you would now like to see him get a couple more – it’s certainly possible for him to do so.

Bradley Barcola gets off the mark for Liverpool with an instinctive finish 🔥 📺 Stream now on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/5K7YBB7UyG

A Van Dijk-esque header you could say, and Liverpool have punished LASK’s jittery set-piece defending. Good delivery from Tsimikas, and Araujo rose highest around seven yards out to plant a header byone Jungwirth.

Some harrying from Gravenberch is enough to win Liverpool another corner, their fifth of the game so far. The goalkeeper was shaky again, but the ball glances off a LASK head and out for another corner.

LASK are targetting Liverpool’s left flank with direct balls forward, and the big centre-forward Adeniran caused Jacquet all manner of problems near the touchline but his touch ran away from him in the box.

The another good Barcola run is found, but his shot is screwed just wide of the near post. Barcola and Wirtz certainly more involved so far.

Diligent defending from Jorgenson to halt the progress of Barcola after a burst into the penalty area from the left. From the Liverpool corner, LASK goalkeeper Jungwirth was uncertain but Araujo could not not get enough on the header.

There really is something incongruous about seeing Kostas Tsimikas wearing the Liverpool captain’s armband. He should never have been given it again after throwing it on the floor after a pre-season friendly in the United States when he, Curtis Jones and Dominik Szoboszlai bickered with each other. The reason Alisson doesn’t wear it is because if there is a decision that requires him to talk to the referee in the opposition area, he would be miles from his own goal and potentially vulnerable. Alisson is the real leader on this pitch for this team.

Liverpool starting to turn their screw now. First, Wirtz skipped through a couple of challenges and fired a low shot straight at the goalkeeper before Ngumoha, playing on the right, drops a shoulder and drives to the byline, standing up a dangerous cross.

Then Wirtz tries another dribble through the middle, but his shot is charged down.

Liverpool struggling to clear their lines from the corner, and Schopf scoops a shot over the bar from the edge of the area.

Nyoni then tries a difficult reverse pass back towards Barcola but overcooks it. Moments before, there was a nice touch from Barcola to bring down a switch of play.

Lewis Koumas looking dangerous again, peeling behind LASK’s defence and rounding the goalkeeper Jungwirth on the corner of the penalty area, but he was forced wide and had to settle for a corner which the goalkeeper claims.

Then LASK pour forward again after a cheap giveaway by Araujo, and the home team win a corner of their own. Lively enough start.

Tsimikas scrambling rather to deal with a cross towards Jorgensen, before Alisson puts Liverpool under pressure with a stray pass, and LASK have a corner. Taken short, and then stood up to the back post but Liverpool clear.

Kostas Tsimikas captains Liverpool tonight, not words I ever expected to type but it is a team short of experience. Liverpool enjoying all of the possession so far, LASK are defending in a 5-2-3 shape, so Liverpool’s full-backs should have some time and space. Gravenberch does well to win a foul in midfield.

The home team play in all red, so Liverpool are in their white away strip. It looks like there is some Liverpool support among the locals/neutrals in the home end.

LASK XI: Jungwirth, Jorgensen, Mbuyamba, Alemao, Andrade, Dibango, Danek, Bogarde, Schopf, Lang, Adeniran

Subs: Schutzenauer, Schillinger, Freckleton, Ljubicic, Kalajdzic, Verhaeghe, Elfadli, Flecker, Kane.

A young Liverpool team has been selected to face Linz – the third youngest, according to Opta, that the club have fielded in the Champions League – and Andoni Iraola is being mindful of players such as Virgil van Dijk and Alexis Mac Allister being overburdened ahead of Saturday’s trip to Brentford.

One novice who certainly deserves his starting spot is Trey Nyoni, the England Under-21 international has impressed in the opportunities he has been given so far this year. Watch out for his calmness on the ball and the efficiency with which he uses it.

He should get more chances in the next 10 days, as it is difficult to see Dominik Szoboszlai being ready at least until the home match against Brighton on Sunday week.

Asked about Liverpool’s youthful team, Iraola said: “For me Trey [Nyoni], [Lewis] Koumas and Rio [Ngumoha] are young players coming in from the academy but they are first team players.

“They are first team players because we trust them, and in our situation, where we have some injuries, and we come from playing three days ago. I think they can play well, and I hope they do well.”

24 - Liverpool's starting XI against LASK has an average age of 24 years and 186 days, their third-youngest ever for a UEFA Champions League game, older only than September 2001 v Borussia Dortmund (24y 136d) and December 2020 v Midtjylland (24y 26d). Knocks. https://t.co/4JeW73N87k

Iraola makes four changes from the defeat by City so in come Frimpong, Tsimikas, Nyoni and Ngumoha.

Subs: Mamardashvili, Woodman, Gomez, Van Dijk, Kerkez, Mac Allister, Munoz, Chambers, McConnell, Danns, Sonni-Lambie, Lucky

Our team to take on LASK ✊ #UCL https://t.co/8vObg7mgLF

It is early days for Bradley Barcola but is has been an underwhelming start to his Liverpool career. The winger was a rotational player at Paris St-Germain, as he is for France, so Liverpool spending £120m is a gamble on his raw athletic attributes and the hope that he pieces everything together.

As Dominic King writes in this piece: “Barcola had no control over the price that Richard Hughes, Liverpool’s former sporting director, brokered with Paris St-Germain for his release. But something he can control is public perception and, with no goals or assists so far, opinions are starting to form.”

Of the five Premier League teams in the Champions League this season, Liverpool have the friendliest league-phase fixtures and they can secure back-to-back wins against Austrian side LASK in this evening’s early kick off.

Having already vanquished one of their pot one opponents by beating Atletico Madrid at Anfield, Andoni Iraola’s team really should be targeting one of the top spots.

They travel to Linz without some key players, though. Alexander Isak, Cody Gakpo and Dominik Szoboszlai missed the defeat by Manchester City and remain sidelined, while Hugo Ekitike is a long-term absentee.

There were positive aspects to Liverpool’s performance against City, but they collapsed like a deck of cards after Ryan Gravenberch’s harsh second yellow card.

Tonight’s game is one they should dominate, and it is a presentable opportunity for Florian Wirtz and Bradley Barcola to kick-start their seasons and respond to the recent criticism of their performances. Iraola hopes to have a stronger squad to choose from at the weekend, when Liverpool face a stringent test at Brentford. This is the second of nine matches in 28 days for Liverpool.

“You don’t have a lot of time to train,” said Iraola. “You try to prepare the games now a lot of times just with the videos and the tactics boards, just a little bit outside. You have to prioritise the freshness of the players.

“Especially now we are playing four games in 10 days, it’s keeping all the legs, all the energy in the games.

LASK are currently third in the Austrian league, but booked their place in this season’s Champions League proper with a remarkable comeback from 4-0 down on aggregate against Celtic.

They have injury problems of their own to contend with George Bello and Moses Usor limping off in the weekend’s defeat by league leaders Rapid Wien and Ramiz Harakate tearing his anterior cruciate ligament in July.

They do play on a grass pitch at the Raiffeisen Arena though Kasper Schmeichel, the former Celtic goalkeeper who was working as a TV pundit for the game, was critical of the playing surface.

Liverpool teenager Trey Nyoni marked his first senior goal for the club with a sublime first-time volley from the edge of the box during Wednesday’s UEFA Champions League clash against Fenerbahçe.

The 19-year-old midfielder broke the deadlock in Istanbul with a moment of pure technical brilliance in the 25th minute.

The attack opened when fellow teenager Rio Ngumoha skipped past a sequence of challenges to carve his way into the penalty area.

After Ngumoha’s initial shot was blocked, Szoboszlai put in a teasing cross in and Fenerbahçe failed to clear the danger, heading the ball out to the edge of the penalty box.

Nyoni met the dropping ball on the full volley, sending a struck effort past Ederson, wrong-footing the goalkeeper via a minor deflection, to net his landmark first goal in red.

The young Liverpool midfielder scores his first professional goal, and he does it on the Champions League stage ?
